The idea belongs to this piece alone: the frame is a fixed area of ocean and the ice inside it is the data. The ice breaks up between 1979 and 2011, gets restacked as a bar chart, and the loss is then shown as a Greenland outline. The film builds to one memorable comparison.

There is real choreography across the frames: ice cracks, drains away, gets rearranged into bars, and the bars turn into the Greenland reveal. Each frame changes the state of the material rather than swapping words.

Orange stencil numerals over the ice reference survey markings or shipping containers, a typographic choice with a point of view. The year sinks under the water as the ice goes, so the type and image work together.
The navy, ice-white and single safety-orange palette is restrained and well motivated. Still, it sits close to the 'one accent colour on a dark ground' formula.

Against it: the small grotesk captions in the top left are set like defaults, and in frame 2 the caption collides with the ice. The ice texture looks procedural and evenly lit, without real specular light or depth. The bar-chart frame is sparse and close to a diagram.
The sourced footnote (NSIDC, Natural Earth) suggests data-journalism rigour, but the overall finish reads as a strong editorial or in-house piece more than top-studio polish.

Each frame is a different photoreal world: a crater filled with a nebula, a nautilus shell on sand, a protoplanetary disk with comets, and the Helix-nebula eye. These are scale-jump match cuts, the core idea of the sequence.
The light is real and motivated: rim light on the shell, raking light across the crater, a volumetric glow from the disk's star. Sand, rock and pearl surfaces read as physical material.
The palette moves on purpose from cool slate through warm sand to a fiery orange and blue, ending on the title.
The type is restrained: wide-tracked caps for COSMOS sit in the gaps around the pupil so the eye works as the O. The credits are small and tucked into negative space.
The cuts go from macro to cosmic and back, which implies choreographed transitions rather than a slideshow.
gaps: The credit type is a thin geometric sans used in a broadcast-generic way, with no typographic voice beyond tracking.
The eye-nebula and the spiral-shell motifs are familiar space-doc imagery, so they surprise less than the best piece of the year would.
The title card relies on a famous Hubble image and some wide letter spacing rather than a designed lockup that shares the frame's depth.

tells: The palette is a high-chroma house style (violet, cyan, magenta, lime) controlled with real discipline, and every scene has its own dominant key colour.

Character design shows consistent rigging and expression across shots, and there is depth in the lighting and soft shadows on the highway.
The scene-to-scene changes imply a lot of animation and a varied camera.
gaps: No type is visible. Its absence suits a narrated explainer, but nothing typographic lifts the frames.
The flat-vector explainer house style is widely imitated, so the frames are well made but stylistically expected.
The ideas are literal (car equals emissions, slider equals choice) rather than an image only this film could have.

tells: A title sequence built on a clear conceit: cosmic forms rhyme with earthly ones. A nebula pools in a rock crater, a nautilus shell sits on wet sand, a protoplanetary disc echoes the shell's spiral, and the Helix Nebula resolves into a human iris. The visual rhyme of eye and cosmos is the payoff.

Photographic light and material: the wet basalt crater rim, real sand micro-texture with footprints, shallow depth of field on the shell, and volumetric glow in the accretion disc. This is high-end VFX with physically motivated light.
Every frame works as a poster, and the scale contrast swings from macro (shell) to galactic (disc) to intimate (eye). That implies a camera journey of pushes and match-cuts.

Typography is a widely tracked geometric sans for the main title, with credits set small with tracked-caps role labels. It is restrained and elegant but conventional for network title design; the type does not interact with the image.
Palette moves from cold slate, to warm sand, to ember-orange around a blue iris. The complementary-colour climax is deliberate.
gaps: Give the typography a stronger idea. The tracked-sans title and corner credits are safe network conventions and never respond to the imagery.
The cosmic-eye ending is a familiar trope. A more surprising final rhyme would raise its originality.
Credit placement is somewhat formulaic (lower-third in every frame). Choreographing credits into the space of each shot would match the ambition of the image-making.

defects: The pairs.jpg frames 1/6 s apart are nearly identical in all three rows. The ice edge and the bar chart barely move, so most shots read as slow drift or held frames rather than animated motion.
The longest shot runs 12.5 s, and per-second change falls to about 8 over the last 3 s, so the close goes static without a clear reason.

The '3.57' stencil is broken up by ice and partly hidden, while '2012' sits apart in white. The caption starts with 'million km² in September 2012…', which leaves the number out of the sentence, so the main figure is split across three elements and hard to parse.
The thin white captions sit directly on busy cracked-ice texture with low contrast (1979, 1990 and 2011 headers), and in 2011 the caption runs into the crack lines.
The orange stencil years have a mottled fill that looks pasted flat over the ice instead of printed into it. Lighting and shading don't affect the type.
The bar chart build (frame 4) leaves half the frame empty for a long beat and appears to fill at a constant, linear rate.
The data shot's bottom edge holds scattered ice-debris noise that fights with the axis labels.
gaps: Timing and choreography: the ice retreat is one slow, uniform recede repeated year after year. There's no acceleration, no break-up event with weight and follow-through, and the 2012 low point doesn't hit harder than the other years. Energy is roughly flat through the middle and drops near the end, with no peak at 60–80%.

Transitions: the jump from the ice map to the bar chart is a hard cut to an unrelated layout. A top studio would turn the ice into the bars (e.g. a floe slicing into a column) so the one material device carries through the structural change.

Sound: the score looks like a sustained harmonic drone pad with three single hits (~4.2 s, 13.1 s, 18.3 s) and one noise swell (24–26.5 s). There's little arrangement, almost no ice-specific sound design (cracks, groans, water), and a narrow dynamic range. The hits match some cuts, but the year changes aren't marked with sound.
